messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At sixty-six, Arthur still feels the ghost of that temperature on his skin whenever the thermostat shifts in a room. He was ten when his stepfather’s hand closed around his forearm in the basement laundry room. The skin had been exactly fifty-eight degrees, a precise, chilling weight that pressed into the boy’s flesh. That specific temperature on the skin is no longer just a detail; it is a tether. When a draft from an open window hits his wrist, a memory of the event comes to mind suddenly, and his own heart begins to race or pound without warning. He is certain that the coldness was a warning. He had come to believe that you never know what can happen next, so he watches for danger before his mind has even caught up to the moment. What frightened him most was not the strike itself, but the sudden, unannounced arrival of a threat that bypassed thought. Over the following years, this pattern settled into a daily rhythm. He avoids his own body by keeping his sleeves pulled down and refusing to check the pulse points on his wrists. In his current role as a software engineer, these habits take root in the open-plan tech floor. He notices potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment: a heavy letter opener on a receptionist’s desk, a fire extinguisher mounted near the break room, the sharp edge of a monitor stand. When a colleague reaches out to tap his shoulder to ask a question about a deployment, his body reacts before he has even had time to think. His startle to touch fires first, jolting him upright. People can't be trusted. He avoids being touched by any form of physical contact with others, so he wears long-sleeved shirts in summer and turns slightly away when someone walks too close. Seeing people that he socialized with before the event now feels like stepping into a room he no longer belongs to. He is permanently an outsider now, watching teams huddle over whiteboards while he types in silence. Constant vigilance means he has to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, so he maps the exits of every conference room and notes the weight of the staplers on every desk. These adjustments accumulated over months and years, reshaping his days. He stopped going to the Friday afternoon beers with his former project leads, leaving them to wonder why he never answered the group chat. His wife began carrying the groceries to the trunk herself because she knew he would flinch if she tried to take a bag from his hands. The isolation was not chosen lightly; it was the only way to keep his nervous system from flooding. He had come to believe that people cannot be trusted to move gently or speak softly, so he kept his distance, protecting a quiet that felt safer than the noise of the world. At sixty-six, Arthur sat in a therapist’s office and placed his hands flat on his knees, not to look at them, but to anchor them. He had finally come to seek help because the weight of watching for threats had grown too heavy to carry alone. He did not know if he wanted to forget the cold hand on his arm or simply learn to live beside it without flinching. He was most afraid of losing the careful control he had built, yet he was hoping, quietly, for a place where he could rest without checking the corners of the room.
